sources.locator: Chapter 3 'Sequences', §3.2-§3.4 (printed pp. 38-47) and §3.7-§3.8 (printed pp. 56-58) read in full; §3.5-§3.6 and §3.9 (printed pp. 47-56, 59-60) read for the scope boundary of the pair

contents.name: §3.2 Definition 3.8: a sequence of reals is a function N -> R, and sequences may be defined recursively
§3.3 Definition 3.10: convergence of a sequence and divergence (the epsilon-N definition)
§3.3 Proposition 3.11: if a sequence converges, its limit is unique
§3.3 Definition 3.12: divergence to +infinity and to -infinity, with the warning that this is not convergence
§3.3 Example 3.13: n^3 -> +infinity, by the Archimedean choice N > M^{1/3}
contents.reason: The item transports the same Archimedean comparison to the square-root sequence, with the cube-root step replaced by the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegative reals.

contents.name: §3.3 Example 3.14: 1/n -> 0, the basic Archimedean convergence proof
§3.3 Example 3.15: the alternating sequence (-1)^{n+1} does not converge
§3.3 Example 3.16: the sequence (1 + 1/n)^n converges to a limit e with 2 < e < 3
contents.reason: The limit is taken as the definition of e on the exponential page, and the bound 2 < e < 3 is the item cor-two-less-than-e-less-than-three there; integer powers and the binomial theorem lie outside this pair's declared prerequisite closure.

contents.name: §3.3 Definition 3.17 and Example 3.18: bounded above, bounded below, bounded, with examples
§3.3 Proposition 3.19: every convergent sequence is bounded
§3.3 tail discussion and Example 3.20: changing the first hundred terms of 1/n to n leaves the sequence bounded and convergent to 0
§3.3 Definition 3.21: a property holds eventually or infinitely often
§3.4 Theorem 3.22: limits of convergent sequences preserve non-strict inequalities
§3.4 Theorem 3.23 (Sandwich): a sequence squeezed between two convergent bounds sharing a limit converges to that limit
§3.4 Example 3.24: the sandwich theorem needs the two bounds to share their limit
§3.4 Corollary 3.25: x_n -> x implies |x_n| -> |x|, by the reverse triangle inequality
§3.4 Theorem 3.26: sums, scalar multiples and products of convergent sequences converge to the expected limits
§3.4 paragraph after Theorem 3.26: the sum of two divergent sequences may converge, with the witness x_n = n, y_n = -n
§3.5-§3.6 monotone sequences, the monotone convergence theorem and the limsup/liminf machinery (Definitions 3.27-3.38, Theorem 3.29, Theorem 3.39 and following)
contents.reason: Monotone convergence, the geometric sequence and the limsup/liminf calculus are built on later pages of the same track, where the required completeness and order tools exist; neither page is inside this pair's declared closure.

contents.name: §3.7 Cauchy sequences: the definition, and the theorem that every convergent sequence is Cauchy
§3.7 the Cauchy criterion (every Cauchy sequence of reals converges) and its consequences
contents.reason: The criterion from the least-upper-bound property is proved on the next page of the track; the construction page already supplies the Cauchy-completeness of the reals it builds.

contents.name: §3.8 Definition 3.48 and Proposition 3.50: subsequences are composites with strictly increasing index maps, and every subsequence of a convergent sequence converges to the same limit
§3.8 Corollary 3.51 and Example 3.52: subsequences with different limits force divergence, exhibited on (-1)^{n+1}
contents.reason: The false statement and its refutation already carry the alternating sequence and the divergence information; the example adds the two-subsequence bookkeeping.

contents.name: §3.9 the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem
contents.reason: The theorem needs the peak or nested-interval completeness machinery of the next page of the track; on this pair's order it is not available and is not used.

sources.title: Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis I: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I (author-hosted complete book PDF, 312 pp.)
sources.locator: Chapter 2, §2.1 'Sequences and limits' and §2.2 'Facts about limits of sequences' (printed pp. 51-71), read in full; §2.1.1-§2.1.3 read for the scope boundary

contents.name: §2.1 Definitions 2.1.1-2.1.2: sequences and convergence, with the quantifier order stressed
§2.1 Example 2.1.3: the constant sequence converges to its value
§2.1 Example 2.1.4: 1/n -> 0 from the Archimedean property
§2.1 Example 2.1.5: (-1)^n diverges, by an epsilon = 1/2 argument
§2.1 Proposition 2.1.6: a convergent sequence has a unique limit
§2.1 Proposition 2.1.7: a convergent sequence is bounded
§2.1 Example 2.1.8: (n^2 + 1)/(n^2 + n) -> 1 by throwing away information for a simpler estimate
§2.1.1 Theorem 2.1.10: a monotone sequence converges iff it is bounded
contents.reason: The monotone convergence theorem is the defining result of the next page of the track, where it is proved from the least-upper-bound property.

contents.name: §2.1.1 Example 2.1.11 and its closing argument: 1/sqrt(n) is decreasing with infimum 0, using sqrt(n+1) >= sqrt(n) and the Archimedean property
contents.reason: The example supplies the inequality sqrt(n+1) >= sqrt(n) and the Archimedean square comparison that the two root examples transpose into divergence and difference statements.

contents.name: §2.1.2 Definition 2.1.14 and Proposition 2.1.15: tails, and convergence depends only on some tail
§2.1.3 subsequences (Definition of subsequence) and Proposition 2.1.17: a convergent sequence has every subsequence convergent to the same limit
§2.1.3 Proposition 2.1.15-adjacent subsequential-limit material and Bolzano-Weierstrass (stated in §2.3)
contents.reason: Subsequential limits and Bolzano-Weierstrass belong to the later pages of the track; this pair only fixes the subsequence vocabulary and the inheritance of limits.

contents.name: §2.1.4 Exercises 2.1.3, 2.1.6 and 2.1.14: (-1)^n/2^n, n/(n^2+1) and convergent subsequences of (-1)^n
contents.reason: The exercises ask for exactly the decisions the two squeeze computations carry out, one null oscillating sequence and one rational expression.

contents.name: §2.1.4 Exercise 2.1.5 and Exercise 2.1.19: n/(n+1) -> 1, and a sequence eventually constant at x converges to x
contents.reason: The expression example generalises Exercise 2.1.5, and Exercise 2.1.19 is the tail phenomenon behind the finite-modification example.

contents.name: §2.1.4 remaining exercises 2.1.1-2.1.2, 2.1.7-2.1.13, 2.1.15-2.1.18 and 2.1.20-2.1.21
contents.reason: Routine drill on the same definitions; several involve integer powers or monotone convergence, which lie outside this pair's declared prerequisite closure, and none is needed by the pair's A page.

contents.name: §2.2 Lemma 2.2.1: the squeeze lemma
§2.2 Example 2.2.2: 1/(n sqrt(n)) -> 0 squeezed between 0 and 1/n
§2.2 Lemma 2.2.3 and Corollary 2.2.4: limits preserve non-strict inequalities and interval bounds
§2.2 the paragraph after Corollary 2.2.4: strict inequalities are not preserved, as -1/n < 1/n with both limits 0
§2.2 Proposition 2.2.5: the algebra of limits, including the quotient clause with its nonzero-limit hypothesis
§2.2 Proposition 2.2.6: limits of powers x_n^k and of k-th roots
contents.reason: Integer and k-th powers are homed on roots-and-rational-powers, outside this pair's declared prerequisite closure; the roots page already proves the corresponding algebra in the reals.

contents.name: §2.2 Proposition 2.2.7 and the worked computation after it: |x_n| -> |x|, and expressions such as 1 + 1/n - 100/n^2 evaluated from known limits
§2.2 the cautionary computation n^2/(n+1) - n -> -1, where the summands diverge
contents.reason: The caution is the same phenomenon as the n, -n witness, with the difference computed by algebra rather than read off.

contents.name: §2.2.3 recursively defined sequences (Examples 2.2.8-2.2.9) and §2.2.4-§2.2.5 the comparison, ratio and root tests (Proposition 2.2.10, Proposition 2.2.11, Examples 2.2.13-2.2.14)
contents.reason: Recursive, geometric and ratio/root-test examples are published on the later pages of the track, where monotone convergence, the Cauchy criterion and general powers are available.

contents.name: §2.2.4 Exercise 2.2.6: z_n = x_n/y_n and w_n = y_n/x_n for x_n = 1/n^2, y_n = 1/n, and whether Proposition 2.2.5 applies
§2.2.5 Exercises 2.2.1-2.2.5, 2.2.7-2.2.11 (excluding 2.2.6)
contents.reason: Exercises on the same algebra, ratio and subsequence tools; none is needed by the A page, and the geometric and power exercises lie outside the pair's declared closure.

contents.name: §3.3 tail discussion and Example 3.20: changing the first hundred terms leaves boundedness, convergence and the limit unchanged

§3.4 Corollary 3.25: |x_n| -> |x| when x_n -> x

§3.4 paragraph after Theorem 3.26: 'the convergence of x_n + y_n does not imply the convergence of x_n and y_n separately; for example x_n = n and y_n = -n'
